name: Provenance of Research Images and Data
title: Provenance of Research Images and Data
answer: Provenance of research images and data covers the origin, custody, and transformation history of visual evidence and datasets used in scholarly work. It includes microscopy images, gel and blot images, medical and satellite imagery, plots, tables, supplementary files, and the raw measurements behind them. It also covers AI generated or AI assisted images and synthetic datasets when they appear in papers or preprints. In a library of 135 research papers and 12,993 extracted claims, provenance is what lets a reader trace a claim back to the figure, table, or dataset that supports it. The scope stops short of judging scientific merit, it records where material came from and what happened to it.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Provenance of research images and data covers the origin, custody, and transformation history of visual evidence and datasets used in scholarly work. It includes microscopy images, gel and blot images, medical and satellite imagery, plots, tables, supplementary files, and the raw measurements behind them. It also covers AI generated or AI assisted images and synthetic datasets when they appear in papers or preprints. In a library of 135 research papers and 12,993 extracted claims, provenance is what lets a reader trace a claim back to the figure, table, or dataset that supports it. The scope stops short of judging scientific merit, it records where material came from and what happened to it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Provenance work runs on repositories, electronic lab notebooks, laboratory information management systems, imaging platforms, and version control systems. It depends on persistent identifiers such as DOIs and ORCID iDs, metadata schemas, checksums, and audit logs that record who did what and when. Image files may carry embedded metadata, content credentials, or sidecar records that describe capture settings, software, and edits. Storage must separate raw data from derived data and keep both available for inspection. The infrastructure is only as good as the habits that feed it, so capture at the point of creation matters more than reconstruction later.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by capturing provenance at the source, assigning identifiers, and recording every processing step in a log. Researchers document instrument settings, software versions, parameters, and the sequence of transformations from raw image to final figure. Checksums and version control help detect changes, while image analysis tools such as ImageJ and Fiji are commonly used to inspect and measure images. Duplicate detection, error level analysis, and noise analysis are used in integrity reviews to look for signs of manipulation or reuse. The method is not a single test, it is a chain of records that lets another person retrace the path.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area cover consent, privacy, copyright, licensing, embargoes, and the terms under which data and images may be shared or reused. Sensitive human data, endangered species locations, and dual use research require controlled access and clear provenance trails. Journals, funders, and institutions set policies for image integrity, data availability, and correction or retraction when provenance cannot be established. Gaps in provenance create risk, including unverifiable findings, wasted effort, reputational harm, and legal exposure. Provenance records also support fair credit by showing who contributed which image, dataset, or analysis.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward automated provenance capture, machine readable metadata, and standards that travel with a file from capture to publication. Content provenance standards such as C2PA aim to make the history of an image verifiable across tools and platforms. AI systems are being used to flag image duplication, splicing, and synthetic content, while also making synthetic images harder to distinguish. Journals and repositories are moving toward routine checks at submission and stronger links between papers, data, and code. The open question is how to keep provenance useful without creating new barriers for legitimate research.
